new_statements.quote: 3.3.1 Stress. Like in other Aslian languages stress has no lexically contrastive function in Maniq and falls invariably on the final syllable. Furthermore, no secondary stress has been found. Thai loans receive stress on the final syllable, consistent with the stress patterns in both Maniq and Thai (Haas 1964). [Wnuk 2016: 62-63: 'As with other Aslian languages, the final syllable is the most stable part of the word ... It always receives primary stress ... Since pre-final syllables are unstressed, vowels are less stable phonetically ... 3.8.3 Stress and tone. Stress invariably falls on the final syllable. Maniq does not employ any suprasegmental features like tone or register for lexical contrast.']
new_statements.citation: Wnuk, Ewelina & Niclas Burenhult. 2014. Contact and isolation in hunter-gatherer language dynamics: Evidence from Maniq phonology (Aslian, Malay Peninsula). Studies in Language 38(4): 956-981. doi:10.1075/sl.38.4.06wnu

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text, PDF page 17 = printed p. 972). Section 3.3 'Prosodic features', 3.3.1 'Stress' reads exactly: "Like in other Aslian languages stress has no lexically contrastive function in Maniq and falls invariably on the final syllable. Furthermore, no secondary stress has been found. Thai loans receive stress on the final syllable, consistent with the stress patterns in both Maniq and Thai (Haas 1964)." -- verbatim as quoted. The following 3.3.2 'Tone' finds no contrastive tone in borrowed or indigenous lexicon, so this is a plain stress language, not tonal/pitch-accent. Corroboration also checked in PDF pp. 84-87 = printed 62-65): p.62 "the final syllable is the most stable par…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and fixed on the final syllable of the word (the stable 'major' syllable, as across Aslian); pre-final syllables are unstressed with reduced, variable vowels; Thai loanwords are likewise final-stressed; no tone or register.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly: 'no secondary stress has been found' (Wnuk & Burenhult 2014: 972).
new_statements.exceptions: None to the final-syllable rule. Proclitics are unstressed and do not affect stress assignment of the host (Wnuk 2016: 65); reduplicative/prefixal pre-final syllables are unstressed; function words unstressed in connected speech but stressed in isolation (2014: 964).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phonology article based on first-hand fieldwork (Wnuk) among Maniq of Satun/Trang/Phatthalung provinces, southern Thailand; phonetic transcriptions mark stress on the final syllable e.g. [pʌ̃ŋ-'pɛɡŋ] 'cheek'. No instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Maniq (autonym maniʔ; also known as Tonga, Mos, Ten'en/Ten-edn, 'Sakai' of Trang/Satun/Phatthalung, southern Thailand), ISO tnz = Glottolog tong1308; Wnuk's fieldwork is with the nomadic Maniq groups of the Banthad mountains (Satun/Trang/Phatthalung). Distinct from Kensiw (kens1248) of Yala, which Bishop 1996 confusingly also labelled 'Maniq'.
